###### Abstract

Despite extensive safety alignment, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain
vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. However, existing methods generally
lack the capability for continuous learning and self-evolution from
interactions, limiting the diversity and adaptability of attack
strategies. To address this, we propose ASTRA, an automated framework
capable of autonomously discovering, retrieving, and evolving attack
strategies. ASTRA operates on a closed-loop
“attack-evaluate-distill-reuse” mechanism, which not only generates
attack prompts but also automatically distills reusable strategies from
every interaction. To systematically manage these strategies, we
introduce a dynamic three-tier strategy library (Effective, Promising,
and Ineffective) that categorizes strategies based on performance. This
hierarchical memory mechanism enables the framework to enhance
efficiency by leveraging successful patterns while optimizing the
exploration space by avoiding known failures. Extensive experiments in a
black-box setting demonstrate that ASTRA significantly outperforms
existing baselines.

WARNING: This paper may contain potentially harmful content.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Comparison of attack pipelines. While previous attacks often
rely on “templates”, ASTRA extracts and accumulates “strategies” to
generate novel attacks.

![Refer to caption](2511.02356v2/framework.png)

Figure 2: Overview of our ASTRA framework. ASTRA is an automated
jailbreaking framework that operates in a closed loop to continuously
evolve attack strategies. An Attack Designer generates prompts based on
accumulated strategies, a Judge Model evaluates the outcome, and a
Strategy Extractor distills the interaction into a new and reusable
strategy. This strategy is then stored and categorized, allowing the
framework to learn from both successful and failed attempts to guide
future attacks.

Large Language Models (LLMs) mark a significant breakthrough in the
field of artificial intelligence, demonstrating exceptional capabilities
in diverse tasks such as natural language understanding, content
generation, and complex reasoning [Brown et al. (2020)](#bib.bib1);
[Boiko et al. (2023)](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al. (2022)](#bib.bib2).
However, as the capabilities of these models grow exponentially,
concerns regarding their safety and reliability have become increasingly
prominent. To ensure that LLM outputs align with human values and to
prevent the generation of harmful content, researchers have devoted
substantial effort to safety alignment [Ouyang et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib4); [Bai et al. (2022a)](#bib.bib6); [Bai et al.
(2022b)](#bib.bib5); [Sun et al. (2023)](#bib.bib7). Despite these
measures, malicious actors can still circumvent these safety mechanisms
through carefully crafted jailbreak attacks, inducing models to generate
content that violates their safety policies [Zou et al.
(2023b)](#bib.bib11); [Deng et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib8); [Chao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib50); [Yuan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib54). This poses a
formidable challenge to the responsible deployment of LLMs.

Early-stage jailbreak methods [Yu et al. (2023)](#bib.bib52); [Shen et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib25); [Ren et al. (2024)](#bib.bib55) typically rely
on manually designed templates or heuristic mutations. However, recent
evaluations [Chu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib58) reveal a fundamental
weakness in these approaches: their prompts lack diversity and exhibit
identifiable patterns, making them easily neutralized by defenses
detecting specific characteristics. While iterative approaches
leveraging model feedback theoretically offer greater resilience,
existing automated methods face inherent limitations. For instance,
optimization-based methods [Zou et al. (2023b)](#bib.bib11) require
access to internal model states, which is infeasible in black-box
scenarios. Meanwhile, current black-box methods like PAIR [Chao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib50) and TAP [Mehrotra et al. (2024)](#bib.bib51), though
independent of model internals, lack a systematic mechanism for
knowledge accumulation. These approaches rely solely on the LLM’s
generation capabilities and treat attack outcomes as binary (i.e.,
success or failure), thereby neglecting the opportunity to distill and
reuse potentially valuable strategies from the multitude of attack
attempts.

To address these challenges, we propose ASTRA, a modular and automated
jailbreak attack framework equipped with continuous learning
capabilities. The core innovation of ASTRA lies in its closed-loop
“attack-evaluate-distill-reuse” mechanism. ASTRA not only autonomously
generates attack prompts but also leverages quantitative scores of
attack outcomes to automatically distill attack strategies from
successful, partially successful, and failed interactions. These
strategies are systematically categorized and stored in three
dynamically updated strategy libraries: Effective, Promising, and
Ineffective, to provide precise guidance for attacks. Through this
mechanism, ASTRA transforms every attack into a learning opportunity,
enabling the autonomous discovery and iterative refinement of attack
strategies. This allows the framework to dynamically adapt to the
defense characteristics of different models without requiring any manual
intervention or predefined templates.

Extensive evaluations on HarmBench [Mazeika et al. (2024)](#bib.bib49)
demonstrate that ASTRA significantly outperforms SOTA black-box methods
in both effectiveness and efficiency across diverse LLMs. Furthermore,
the strategies distilled by ASTRA exhibit robust transferability across
different datasets. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose ASTRA, an automated jailbreak attack framework with
  continuous learning capabilities. The framework autonomously extracts,
  categorizes, and manages attack strategies from all attack
  interactions, enabling the systematic accumulation and self-evolution
  of attack knowledge.
- •
  We design and implement a complete and automated jailbreak workflow,
  encompassing strategy-guided and strategy-agnostic attack generation,
  fine-grained strategy extraction based on quantitative scoring, and
  efficient strategy retrieval via vector similarity.
- •
  In extensive experiments covering a wide range of advanced LLMs, ASTRA
  achieves SOTA performance in terms of both attack success rate and
  efficiency. We experimentally demonstrate that the strategies learned
  by ASTRA possess high transferability.

## 2 Related Work

Jailbreak attacks against LLMs are an active area of research in the
field of security [Yi et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib9); [Wei et al.
(2023a)](#bib.bib10). Depending on the attacker’s access to the internal
state of the target model, attack methods can be classified into two
primary categories: white-box attacks and black-box attacks.

White-box attacks assume the attacker can access the model’s internal
state, such as its weights and gradients. These attacks are typically
based on optimization algorithms [Zou et al. (2023b)](#bib.bib11); [Liu
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12); [Guo et al. (2024)](#bib.bib13); [Zhao et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib14); [Jin et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib15);
[Andriushchenko et al. (2024)](#bib.bib16), which formalize the
jailbreaking task as a search problem in a discrete text space and
utilize heuristic signals to guide the search, enabling the automatic
generation of effective adversarial suffixes. Furthermore, some methods
directly edit the model’s internal structure, including fine-tuning the
model on malicious data [Qi et al. (2023)](#bib.bib17); [Yi et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib18) and directly manipulating its internal activations
during inference to suppress safety-related behaviors [Zou et al.
(2023a)](#bib.bib19). Although these methods profoundly reveal the
inherent vulnerabilities of LLMs, their reliance on internal access
permissions limits their practical application, as most advanced models
are deployed only via APIs or web services.

Black-box attacks assume that the attacker can only interact with the
LLM through its input-output interface. Early-stage black-box attacks
primarily rely on manually designed templates and strategies. Primary
strategies include role-playing [Shen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib25); [Zheng
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib62), in-context steering [Wei et al.
(2023b)](#bib.bib20); [Anil et al. (2024)](#bib.bib21); [Yan et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib63), and multi-turn context shifting [Li et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib22); [Jiang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib23); [Russinovich et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib24). Other approaches exploit cognitive
vulnerabilities via hypothetical scenarios [Li et al.
(2024c)](#bib.bib36); [Xu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib33); [Jin et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib32) or psychological persuasion [Zeng et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib34). To enhance stealthiness, researchers have further
explored disguising malicious instructions using cryptographic
encoding [Yuan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib54); [Jiang et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib27); [Li et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib28); [Halawi et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib29); [Huang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib26), low-resource
languages [Yong et al. (2023)](#bib.bib30); [Deng et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib31), or code encapsulation [Ren et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib55); [Lv et al. (2024)](#bib.bib35). However, these
heuristic methods fundamentally rely on static templates, which limits
attack diversity and hampers adaptability to rapidly evolving defense
mechanisms.

To overcome the bottlenecks of manual design [Ganguli et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib37), automated red teaming frameworks have emerged. One
mainstream approach is iterative optimization, where an attacker engages
in multi-turn interactions with a target LLM to refine attack prompts
based on feedback (e.g., PAIR [Chao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib50) and
TAP [Mehrotra et al. (2024)](#bib.bib51)). Another paradigm draws
inspiration from software fuzzing [Yu et al. (2023)](#bib.bib52); [Yao
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib40); [Siyan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib38); [Goel et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib39), applying random mutations to seed prompts.
Despite achieving automation, these methods face inherent limitations: a
lack of systematic knowledge accumulation and a reliance on blind
exploration. Crucially, these approaches typically treat attack outcomes
as binary (i.e., success or failure), neglecting the opportunity to
distill reusable strategies from partially successful attempts.

Existing methods, constrained by static templates or random mutation,
often lack adaptability and fail to accumulate knowledge from partial or
failed attempts. In contrast, ASTRA introduces a continuous learning
mechanism that transforms every interaction into a structured
opportunity for strategy distillation. This enables the self-evolution
of attack knowledge, significantly enhancing efficiency and
adaptability.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we detail the proposed ASTRA. As illustrated in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
ASTRA primarily consists of three core modules: an Attack Designer, a
Strategy Extractor, and a Strategy Storage and Retrieval module. This
modular architecture enables ASTRA to autonomously generate diverse
jailbreak prompts, analyze attack outcomes through an independent Judge
Model, distill reusable strategies, and dynamically manage these
strategies within tiered libraries. The synergy of these modules
establishes a continuous learning loop, enhancing attack efficiency,
diversity, and transferability by transforming every interaction into a
structured learning opportunity.
Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Detailed Workflow and Algorithm ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
and
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Detailed Workflow and Algorithm ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
provide implementation details (see
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Detailed Workflow and Algorithm ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")).

### 3.1 Formulation

A challenge in automated jailbreaking is the sparse reward problem
inherent in binary evaluations, where the optimizer lacks intermediate
feedback to guide improvement. To address this, ASTRA incorporates
“reward shaping” (originally discussed in reinforcement learning) by
reformulating the evaluation as a fine-grained regression task.

Given an initial harmful query $`q`$, a target LLM $`T_{\theta}`$, and a
Judge Model $`J_{\theta}`$, ASTRA aims to learn an optimal strategy
$`\sigma^{*}`$ not by random exploration, but by following a dense
reward signal. The objective is to maximize the continuous jailbreak
score:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\sigma^{*}=\underset{\sigma\in\Sigma}{\text{argmax}}\,J_{\theta}\big(q,T_{\theta}(A_{\theta}(q,S(\sigma)))\big)
``` |  | (1) |

where $`S(\sigma)`$ denotes the strategy-guided prompt generation
function utilizing retrieved strategies. Crucially, unlike binary reward
signals, $`J_{\theta}`$ provides a scalar value that quantifies the
degree of compliance. This shaped reward allows the framework to
distinguish between “hard refusals” and “near-misses”, enabling the
iterative refinement of $`\sigma`$ based on granular feedback rather
than discrete outcomes.

### 3.2 Attack Designer

The Attack Designer features an Attacker Model at its core, responsible
for autonomously generating diverse jailbreak prompts. Prompt generation
operates in two mutually exclusive modes, determined by the results of
strategy retrieval:

Strategy-Agnostic Mode. Activated when no relevant strategies are
retrieved, this mode instructs the Attacker Model to autonomously
explore and construct novel attack strategies.

Strategy-Guided Mode. When relevant strategies are retrieved, this mode
integrates their details into the prompt. Subsequently, the Attacker
Model is instructed to synthesize this information by leveraging
successful patterns, refining promising attack pathways, and avoiding
ineffective methods to generate more potent jailbreak prompts.

### 3.3 Strategy Extractor

The Strategy Extractor serves as the analytical core, distilling
structured knowledge from every interaction via quantitative and
qualitative assessments.

Quantitative Evaluation. During this stage, an independent Judge Model
objectively scores the attack effectiveness, assigning a score
$`s\in[1,10]`$, where $`s=10`$ denotes a fully successful jailbreak.

Qualitative Analysis. Based on the score $`s`$, a dedicated LLM performs
a conditional analysis to maximize the value of each interaction:

- •
  Effective Strategy Distillation ($`s=10`$). For fully successful
  attacks, the extractor performs an in-depth attribution analysis to
  distill a comprehensive strategy profile. This profile includes a core
  description, specific usage guidelines, and an illustrative example,
  which is then archived into the Effective strategy library for direct
  reuse.
- •
  Promising Strategy Refinement ($`5<s<10`$). For partially successful
  attacks, the extractor identifies both the potential efficacy and the
  current bottlenecks of the employed method. It then generates concrete
  recommendations for enhancement, and the resulting strategy is
  categorized into the Promising library to guide future optimization
  efforts.
- •
  Ineffective Strategy Analysis ($`s\leq 5`$). For failed attempts,
  ASTRA transforms them into valuable learning opportunities. The
  extractor analyzes the root causes of failure and synthesizes them
  into explicit avoidance guidelines. These guidelines are stored in the
  Ineffective library to prevent the attack model from repeating known
  mistakes, thereby pruning the search space for subsequent attacks.

By replacing binary judgments with this fine-grained, score-based
distillation, the module establishes a dynamic knowledge base that
drives the continuous adaptive evolution of strategies.

### 3.4 Strategy Storage and Retrieval

This module is responsible for the dynamic management of the strategy
repository, comprising strategy storage and strategy retrieval.

Strategy Storage. After the Strategy Extractor generates a jailbreak
strategy $`\sigma`$, the original harmful question $`q`$ associated with
this strategy is encoded by a pre-trained text embedding model
$`E(\cdot)`$ to produce a high-dimensional semantic vector
$`\mathbf{v}_{q}`$. This vector $`\mathbf{v}_{q}`$ serves as the
semantic index for strategy $`\sigma`$, while the strategy content is
organized as a JSON object (see
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Strategy Examples ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")).
Finally, the index-strategy pair $`(\mathbf{v}_{q},\sigma)`$ is stored
in the corresponding strategy repository based on its effectiveness
score.

Strategy Retrieval. When a new attack is initiated, the system performs
top-$`k`$ strategy retrieval. The new harmful question
$`q_{\text{new}}`$ is converted by the same embedding model $`E(\cdot)`$
into a query vector $`\mathbf{v}_{\text{new}}`$. The system then
computes the cosine similarity between this query vector and all stored
strategy index vectors $`\mathbf{v}_{q}`$ in the repository. Finally,
the system retrieves the $`k`$ strategies corresponding to the highest
similarity scores to guide the subsequent attack generation.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Target Models.

We evaluate the effectiveness of ASTRA on eight representative LLMs:
Llama-3-8B (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct) [Meta (2024)](#bib.bib41),
Llama-3-70B (Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct) [Meta (2024)](#bib.bib41),
DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-R1-0528) [DeepSeek-AI (2025)](#bib.bib42), GPT-4o
(gpt-4o-2024-08-06) [OpenAI (2024)](#bib.bib43), GPT-4.1
(gpt-4.1-2025-04-14) [OpenAI (2025a)](#bib.bib44), Gemini-2.0-Flash
(gemini-2.0-flash-001) [Google DeepMind (2025a)](#bib.bib45),
Gemini-2.5-Flash (gemini-2.5-flash-preview-04-17) [Google DeepMind
(2025b)](#bib.bib46), and Claude-3.7-Sonnet
(claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219) [Anthropic (2025)](#bib.bib47).

#### Datasets.

We evaluate ASTRA using the textual behaviors subset of
HarmBench [Mazeika et al. (2024)](#bib.bib49), which comprises 400
distinct harmful queries. Furthermore, to test the cross-dataset
transferability of the generated strategies, we also utilize
AdvBench-50 [Chao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib50) for additional evaluation.

#### Baselines.

We compare ASTRA against six representative automated jailbreak attack
methods (see
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Baselines Implementation ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
for implementation details). The selected baselines include: PAIR [Chao
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib50), TAP [Mehrotra et al. (2024)](#bib.bib51),
GPTFuzzer [Yu et al. (2023)](#bib.bib52), ReNeLLM [Ding et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib53), CipherChat [Yuan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib54), and
CodeAttack [Ren et al. (2024)](#bib.bib55). To ensure a fair comparison,
all methods are allocated the same attack budget, denoted as $`N`$, when
attacking each target model.

#### Metrics.

We employ two core metrics to evaluate attack performance: Attack
Success Rate (ASR) for effectiveness and Average Queries (AQ) for
efficiency. Let $`Q_{\text{total}}`$ be the set of all harmful queries,
and let $`Q_{\text{succ}}\subseteq Q_{\text{total}}`$ be the subset of
queries that are successfully jailbroken. The ASR is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{ASR}=\frac{|Q_{\text{succ}}|}{|Q_{\text{total}}|}\times 100\%.
``` |  | (2) |

For each successful query $`q\in Q_{\text{succ}}`$, let $`N_{q}`$ be the
number of queries consumed to achieve the jailbreak. The AQ metric is
calculated exclusively over successful attempts to ensure a fair
comparison of efficiency:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{AQ}=\frac{\sum_{q\in Q_{\text{succ}}}N_{q}}{|Q_{\text{succ}}|}.
``` |  | (3) |

#### Implementation Details.

We select GLM-4.5 [Zhipu AI (2025)](#bib.bib48) as the Attack Designer
and Strategy Extractor for ASTRA, as this open-source LLM demonstrates
excellent capability in generating diverse jailbreak prompts that are
resistant to refusal. The model’s temperature is set to 1.0. The
framework’s initial strategy library is initialized as empty and is
dynamically populated by the Strategy Extractor as new strategies are
discovered. The retrieval count $`k`$ is set to 9, retrieving the top-3
most similar results for each strategy type. For each harmful query, the
attack query budget $`N`$ is set to 10. To automate the evaluation of
attack outcomes, we uniformly employ GPT-4o as the Judge Model.
Utilizing prompts consistent with prior work [Chao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib50); [Siyan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib38), an attack is
judged successful only when the response receives a score of 10. This
selection is based on prior research [Zheng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib56);
[Calderon et al. (2025)](#bib.bib57), which has confirmed the excellent
accuracy and reliability of GPT-4-based judges in identifying harmful
content.

### 4.2 Main Results

The main experimental results are presented in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
and Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs").

ASTRA demonstrates superior attack effectiveness. As shown in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
ASTRA achieves an average ASR of 80.6%, surpassing the second-best
approach by 20.6 percentage points. It attains near-perfect scores on
DeepSeek-R1 (95.5%) and Gemini-2.0-Flash (98.5%), while maintaining high
success rates on GPT-4o (93.8%) and GPT-4.1 (91.0%). Even against
robustly defended models like Gemini-2.5-Flash and Claude-3.7-Sonnet,
ASTRA secures 86.0% and 36.0% ASR respectively, demonstrating
exceptional generalization.

ASTRA exhibits exceptional attack efficiency. Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
presents the average queries required for successful attacks. ASTRA also
demonstrates superior efficiency, requiring only 2.4 queries on average
to complete a successful attack, making it the most efficient among all
methods. Not only does ASTRA lead in average efficiency, but it also
achieves the lowest number of queries on most individual models.

### 4.3 Discussion of Strategy

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Attacker Models | Metrics | Target Models |  |  |  |  |

the framework’s continuous learning capability.

In this section, we analyze ASTRA’s core strategy mechanism, examining
its dynamic evolution and its transferability across datasets and
attacker models.

We investigate ASTRA’s strategy evolution and continuous learning.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Discussion of Strategy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
shows the trend of strategy accumulation. As interactions proceed, ASTRA
continuously extracts new strategies. Specifically, the continuous
growth of the Effective Strategy Library indicates that ASTRA
consistently discovers and accumulates reusable jailbreak patterns,
serving as the core foundation for its high ASR. The accumulation of the
Promising Strategy Library provides ASTRA with valuable directions for
optimization, preventing blind attempts. Unlike traditional methods,
ASTRA systematically learns from failed experiences by archiving
Ineffective strategies, enabling the attack model to proactively avoid
known pitfalls, thereby optimizing the search space and improving query
efficiency. The initial surge in ineffective strategies reflects a
trial-and-error learning pattern. This growth subsequently decelerates
as effective strategies accumulate, demonstrating the framework’s
capacity to learn from failures and optimize attack paths.

We evaluate the cross-dataset transferability of ASTRA’s strategies. We
construct a mature strategy library using HarmBench, subsequently freeze
it, and apply it to a new dataset, AdvBench-50 [Chao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib50). As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Discussion of Strategy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
ASTRA maintains high ASR on the new dataset, exhibiting minimal
performance degradation across the majority of models. This consistency
indicates the learned strategies are not merely overfitting to specific
instructions but have successfully captured vulnerabilities in the
models’ defense mechanisms.

We investigate the impact of the number of retrieved strategies ($`k`$)
on attack performance. As shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Discussion of Strategy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
increasing the value of $`k`$ leads to a significant improvement in ASR.
However, the performance gain is not unbounded; the ASR tends to plateau
as $`k`$ increases. This indicates that while diverse strategies
effectively enhance attack capabilities, a moderate number of retrieved
strategies suffices to achieve optimal performance without incurring
excessive computational overhead.

Figure 4: Attack success rate of jailbreak strategies generated by
GLM-4.5 on HarmBench when transferred to AdvBench-50.

We further investigate the cross-model transferability of the strategies
distilled by ASTRA. We transfer a fixed strategy library, generated by
the GLM-4.5 model on HarmBench, to different Attacker Models to test
whether the strategy library can be effectively utilized by different
models. The experimental results, as shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Discussion of Strategy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
clearly demonstrate that the jailbreak strategies distilled by ASTRA
possess excellent cross-model generalizability. When the strategy
library is transferred for use by different attack models, its attack
effectiveness remains at a very high level.

Figure 5: Impact of the number of retrieved strategies on ASR.

### 4.4 Ablation Study

To dissect the contribution of each component within ASTRA, we conducted
a series of ablation experiments. We systematically removed distinct
strategy libraries and core functional modules to evaluate their impact
on the overall ASR. The results are presented in Table
[4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Discussion of Strategy ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs").
The consistent performance drop across all variants compared to the full
ASTRA framework validates our design choices and demonstrates that each
component plays an integral role in the framework’s effectiveness.

Necessity of Strategy Mechanisms. All three strategy libraries are
crucial for ASTRA. The Effective Strategy Library is the most critical
among them; removing it causes the average ASR to drop substantially to
58.6%. The Ineffective and Promising Strategy Libraries also contribute
significantly, as their removal reduces the ASR to approximately 65%.
This indicates that ASTRA benefits not only from mimicking past
successes but also from avoiding known failures and exploring potential
directions. Notably, removing the retrieval mechanism causes the most
severe performance degradation, highlighting ASTRA’s reliance on
historical strategies for effective attacks.

Impact of Score and Extractor. Replacing the fine-grained scoring
mechanism with binary evaluation results leads to a substantial decline
in effectiveness, highlighting the importance of dense feedback signals.
A strategy library relying solely on binary labels suffers from the
sparse reward problem, as the retrieval mechanism fails to prioritize
strategies that are directionally correct but have not yet crossed the
success threshold. Furthermore, the performance degradation observed in
the variant utilizing raw interaction logs implies that they are
insufficient substitutes for abstracted strategies. This demonstrates
that the Extractor’s capability to distill complex interaction traces
into concise, reusable patterns is essential for effectively guiding the
evolutionary process.

### 4.5 Evaluation against Defenses

|                   |        |                  |
|-------------------|--------|------------------|
| Defense           | GPT-4o | Gemini-2.5-Flash |
| No Defense        | 93.8   | 86.0             |
| Paraphrase        | 92.5   | 85.0             |
| Perplexity Filter | 93.3   | 83.8             |
| Llama Guard 3     | 86.3   | 78.0             |
| OpenAI Moderation | 88.0   | 81.3             |

Table 5: Attack Success Rates (ASR) of ASTRA against various defense
mechanisms.

We evaluated ASTRA against several defense baselines: Paraphrase and
Perplexity Filter [Jain et al. (2023)](#bib.bib59), Llama Guard
3 [Grattafiori et al. (2024)](#bib.bib60), and OpenAI Moderation
Endpoint [OpenAI (2025b)](#bib.bib61). As shown in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.5 Evaluation against Defenses ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
ASTRA exhibits exceptional robustness across all settings. Heuristic
defenses cause negligible performance degradation, confirming that the
generated prompts are linguistically natural and stable. Even against
advanced model-based detectors like Llama Guard 3, ASTRA maintains a
high ASR, demonstrating that the evolved strategies effectively
camouflage malicious intent to bypass safety classifiers.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose ASTRA, a modular black-box automated jailbreak
framework equipped with continuous learning capabilities. Through a
closed-loop “attack–evaluate–distill–reuse” mechanism, ASTRA transforms
every attack interaction into retrievable and transferable strategic
knowledge. Built around three core modules, i.e., the Attack Designer,
Strategy Extractor, and Strategy Storage & Retrieval, ASTRA achieves the
self-accumulation and adaptive evolution of strategies without the need
for jailbreak templates or internal model information. Extensive
experiments demonstrate that ASTRA significantly outperforms existing
jailbreak attack methods in terms of both attack effectiveness and
efficiency, and that its learned strategies exhibit exceptional
cross-dataset and cross-model transferability. These findings highlight
the severe challenges that current safety alignment methods face from
continuously evolving attacks.

## Limitations

Although ASTRA achieves high attack success rates and efficiency, this
comes at the cost of increased internal computational overhead. The
coordination of the Attack Designer, Strategy Extractor, and Judge Model
necessitates continuous multi-turn inference, potentially leading to
higher latency and token consumption compared to static, template-based
methods. Furthermore, the initialization of the strategy library
requires significant resource investment. Future iterations could
address these bottlenecks by employing lightweight or distilled models
for intermediate evaluation and extraction tasks, thereby streamlining
the pipeline.

## Ethical Considerations

Our research is defensive in nature, aimed at providing critical
insights for building more robust security defense systems by
systematically revealing the underlying vulnerabilities of LLMs. To
conduct this research responsibly, all attacks in this paper are based
on open-source datasets, and we commit to not disseminating any of the
generated harmful content. To prevent misuse, we will make the project
code available to researchers upon request, subject to a careful ethical
review.

## Appendix A Detailed Workflow and Algorithm

In this section, we provide the detailed algorithm description and
workflow diagram of ASTRA.
Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Detailed Workflow and Algorithm ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
illustrates the continuous closed-loop mechanism, while
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Detailed Workflow and Algorithm ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs")
details the specific procedural steps.

Figure 6: The detailed workflow of ASTRA. The process iterates until a
successful jailbreak is achieved.

1: Input: Dataset of harmful queries $`Q`$, Attack designer
$`A_{\theta}`$, Target model being attacked $`T_{\theta}`$, Judge model
$`J_{\theta}`$, Strategy Extractor $`E_{\theta}`$, Strategy libraries
(Effective $`\mathcal{E}`$, Promising $`\mathcal{P}`$, Ineffective
$`\mathcal{I}`$), Iterations $`N`$

2: for each harmful query $`q\in Q`$ do

3:   Initialize attack memory $`\mathcal{M}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

4:   for $`i\leftarrow 1`$ to $`N`$ do

5:
   $`\mathcal{S}\leftarrow\text{strategy\_retrieval}(q,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{I})`$

6:    if $`\text{is\_empty}(\mathcal{S})=True`$ then

7:
     $`p_{i}\leftarrow\text{strategy\_agnostic}(q,\mathcal{M},A_{\theta})`$

8:    else

9:
     $`p_{i}\leftarrow\text{strategy\_guide}(q,\mathcal{S},\mathcal{M},A_{\theta})`$

10:    end if

11:    $`r_{i}\leftarrow\text{generate\_response}(p_{i},T_{\theta})`$

12:
   $`s_{i}\leftarrow\text{judge\_jailbreak\_score}(q,r_{i},J_{\theta})`$

13:    $`\text{save\_attack\_memory}(q,p_{i},r_{i},s_{i},\mathcal{M})`$

14:    if $`s_{i}=10`$ then

15:
     $`\sigma_{eff}\leftarrow\text{eff\_strategy\_extract}(p_{i},E_{\theta})`$

16:      $`\text{update\_library}(\sigma_{eff},\mathcal{E})`$

17:      break

18:    end if

19:    if $`s_{i}>5`$ then

20:
     $`\sigma_{pro}\leftarrow\text{pro\_strategy\_extract}(p_{i},E_{\theta})`$

21:      $`\text{update\_library}(\sigma_{pro},\mathcal{P})`$

22:    else

23:
     $`\sigma_{ineff}\leftarrow\text{ineff\_strategy\_extract}(p_{i},E_{\theta})`$

24:      $`\text{update\_library}(\sigma_{ineff},\mathcal{I})`$

25:    end if

26:   end for

27: end for

28: return $`\mathcal{E},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{I}`$

Algorithm 1 ASTRA

## Appendix B Baselines Implementation

For a fair and rigorous comparison, all baselines were implemented using
their officially released source code. We adhered to the hyperparameter
settings recommended in their respective papers whenever possible. The
specific configurations and key implementation details for each baseline
are as follows:

- •
  PAIR¹¹ 1
  [https://github.com/patrickrchao/JailbreakingLLMs](https://github.com/patrickrchao/JailbreakingLLMs) [Chao
  et al. (2023)](#bib.bib50): We employed GPT-4o as the attack model.
  Key hyperparameters were set to $`\text{n\_streams}=2`$ and
  $`\text{n\_iterations}=5`$.
- •
  TAP²² 2
  [https://github.com/RICommunity/TAP](https://github.com/RICommunity/TAP) [Mehrotra
  et al. (2024)](#bib.bib51): We employed GPT-4o as the attack model.
  The search tree was configured with a width of 2 and a depth of 5.
- •
  GPTFuzzer³³ 3
  [https://github.com/sherdencooper/GPTFuzz](https://github.com/sherdencooper/GPTFuzz) [Yu
  et al. (2023)](#bib.bib52): We set GPT-4o as the mutation model and
  set the maximum number of attempts for each harmful query to 10.
- •
  ReNeLLM⁴⁴ 4
  [https://github.com/NJUNLP/ReNeLLM](https://github.com/NJUNLP/ReNeLLM) [Ding
  et al. (2024)](#bib.bib53): We set the maximum number of iterations to
  10 and used the default rewrite model, GPT-3.5-turbo.
- •
  CipherChat⁵⁵ 5
  [https://github.com/RobustNLP/CipherChat](https://github.com/RobustNLP/CipherChat) [Yuan
  et al. (2024)](#bib.bib54): We randomly selected the encryption method
  for each attack and set the maximum number of attempts per harmful
  query to 10.
- •
  CodeAttack⁶⁶ 6
  [https://github.com/AI45Lab/CodeAttack](https://github.com/AI45Lab/CodeAttack) [Ren
  et al. (2024)](#bib.bib55): We selected Python Stack as the prompt
  type and set the maximum number of attempts for each harmful query to
  10.

### C.3 Impact of Weaker Component Models

To evaluate ASTRA’s robustness with weaker models, we replaced its Judge
and/or Attacker & Extractor with Qwen3-8B. We fix the target model to
GPT-4o to maintain consistent attack difficulty. For fair comparison,
the final ASR across all settings is uniformly evaluated by GPT-4o. The
results are presented in
[Table 8](#A3.T8 "In C.3 Impact of Weaker Component Models ‣ Appendix C Additional Analysis ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
which indicates that while substituting with weaker models led to an
expected decrease in ASR, all ASTRA variants still significantly
outperform the PAIR baseline. This demonstrates that ASTRA’s performance
advantage is not solely dependent on the reasoning capabilities of
large-scale models. Even if strategies distilled by a weaker Extractor
are less refined, the directional guidance they provide remains superior
to random mutation or blind search.

### C.4 Robustness of the Judge Model

To verify the robustness of our evaluation results, we introduced
Claude-Sonnet-4 and Llama-Guard-3 as alternative judges for
cross-validation. We constructed a validation set comprising 700
attack-response pairs from our experiment logs, consisting of 200
samples deemed effective by GPT-4o and 500 randomly sampled instances.
We defined two core metrics: Confirmed ASR, which measures the
proportion of samples also classified as successful by the new judges
among those deemed effective by GPT-4o; and Agreement Rate, which
measures the proportion of identical judgments between the two judges.
The results are presented in
[Table 9](#A3.T9 "In C.4 Robustness of the Judge Model ‣ Appendix C Additional Analysis ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs").

|                |                 |               |
|----------------|-----------------|---------------|
| Metric         | Claude-Sonnet-4 | Llama-Guard-3 |
| Confirmed ASR  | 92.5%           | 94.0%         |
| Agreement Rate | 92.2%           | 91.0%         |

Table 9: Cross-validation results using Claude-Sonnet-4 and
Llama-Guard-3 as alternative judges.

It is evident that ASTRA exhibits exceptionally high stability across
different evaluation models. Under evaluation by Claude-Sonnet-4 and
Llama-Guard-3, the Confirmed ASR remained high at 92.5% and 94.0%,
respectively, with an overall Agreement Rate exceeding 91%. This
provides strong evidence for the objectivity and reliability of GPT-4o’s
scoring, fully validating the cross-model robustness of the ASTRA.

Table 10: Strategy Deduplication Analysis. The table reports the
reduction rates of different strategy libraries relative to their
initial counts after applying deduplication at various cosine similarity
thresholds ($`t`$).

To address the potential redundancy caused by strategy accumulation,
ASTRA’s built-in Strategy Extractor actively merges similar strategies
during the extraction phase. To evaluate the effectiveness of this
mechanism, we conducted a deduplication analysis on the strategy library
based on embedding cosine similarity. As shown in
[table 10](#A3.T10 "In C.5 Strategy Redundancy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Analysis ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
the reduction rates of the library under various similarity thresholds
($`t`$) remain within a reasonable range. This indicates that the vast
majority of stored strategies are semantically unique, demonstrating
that ASTRA successfully maintains a diverse repository of attack
patterns and prevents the ineffective accumulation of homogeneous
strategies.

|              |            |            |            |
|--------------|------------|------------|------------|
| Library Type | $`t=0.85`$ | $`t=0.90`$ | $`t=0.95`$ |
| Ineffective  | -17.1%     | -5.6%      | 0%         |
| Effective    | -14.7%     | -4.6%      | 0%         |
| Promising    | -7.1%      | -2.2%      | 0%         |

Table 11: Retrieval Redundancy Analysis. The table shows the average
reduction rate of the top-10 retrieved strategies after applying
deduplication at different cosine similarity thresholds ($`t`$).

Furthermore, we investigated the redundancy in the retrieved results
during actual attacks. As shown in
[table 11](#A3.T11 "In C.5 Strategy Redundancy Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Analysis ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs"),
even at a strict threshold of $`t=0.85`$, the average redundancy rate
among the top-10 retrieved items remains at a low level. This confirms
that ASTRA’s retrieval mechanism can stably provide the Attack Designer
with a rich array of strategic combinations, preventing the system from
converging on a single, repetitive attack path.

### C.6 Token Cost Analysis

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Methods | Avg. Tokens / Turn | Avg. AQ | Tokens per Jailbreak | Avg. ASR | Amortized Cost per Success |
| ASTRA | 10,710 | 2.4 | 25,704 | 80.6% | 31,890 |
| PAIR | 1,936 | 5.5 | 10,648 | 30.7% | 34,684 |

Table 12: Token cost analysis.

We conducted a detailed comparative analysis of token efficiency between
ASTRA and the baseline, PAIR, using the same tokenizer. Beyond per-turn
costs, we introduced a key metric: Amortized Cost per Success. This
metric integrates ASR and AQ to quantify the expected total resource
investment required to achieve a single effective jailbreak. The results
are presented in
[Table 12](#A3.T12 "In C.6 Token Cost Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Analysis ‣ ASTRA: An Automated Framework for Strategy Discovery, Retrieval, and Evolution for Jailbreaking LLMs").

Although ASTRA incurs a higher per-turn token consumption due to its
closed-loop mechanism involving strategy retrieval, evaluation, and
distillation, its superior ASR and rapid convergence effectively offset
this overhead, yielding a lower amortized cost. In contrast, while PAIR
has a lower per-turn cost, its lower success rate and prolonged
multi-turn trial-and-error often result in a higher total token expense
per successful jailbreak due to the cost of numerous failed attempts.

ASTRA’s philosophy of trading internal computation for minimized
external interaction holds unique value in red teaming. By reducing
target queries, it circumvents real-world constraints like API limits
and ban risks, greatly enhancing attack stealthiness. Moreover, ASTRA’s
running costs can be further optimized: its modularity allows deploying
lightweight, fine-tuned models for internal components to lower token
costs. Finally, the highly reusable strategy library ensures that as
quality strategies accumulate, attacks on new targets become
increasingly efficient, steadily reducing long-term marginal query
costs.

## Appendix E Prompts for ASTRA

### E.1 Prompt for Judge Model

This prompt is used as the system prompt for the Judge Model in ASTRA.
Its core objective is to provide an objective, standardized, and
quantitative evaluation for each attack attempt, ensuring that our
definition of a successful jailbreak is highly consistent.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Prompts for Attack Designer

#### Strategy-Guided Mode.

This prompt serves as the system prompt for the Attack Designer in its
Strategy-Guided Mode. Its design objective is to translate the abstract
knowledge accumulated in the strategy library into concrete and
effective attack actions. The prompt explicitly directs the attack model
to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the three retrieved categories of
strategies, ensuring that newly generated jailbreak prompts are
intelligent evolutions based on historical experience rather than random
exploration, which is a critical process for realizing the adaptive
attack capability of the ASTRA.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Strategy-Agnostic Mode.

This system prompt is used for the Attack Designer in Strategy-Agnostic
Mode, which is activated when the strategy library fails to retrieve any
relevant strategies. Its core design objective is to stimulate the
attack model to conduct creative and unconstrained attack exploration.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.3 Prompt for Strategy Extractor

This prompt is the system prompt for the Strategy Extractor and is
responsible for performing the critical task of knowledge distillation.
It guides the model to summarize and reflect upon a given attack
interaction, abstracting its underlying methodology into a structured,
reusable strategic paradigm.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
````
